name: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia (ARSACS / SACS)
aliases: autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxias are a group in which cerebellar ataxia combines with pyramidal spasticity; the prototype is ARSACS, caused by biallelic variants in SACS, which encodes the chaperone-like protein sacsin
ARSACS classically presents in early childhood with a triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-limb spasticity and a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy
A characteristic feature is thickening of the retinal nerve fibres, demonstrable on fundoscopy or optical coherence tomography
Brain MRI often shows superior cerebellar vermian atrophy together with linear pontine hypointensities and a bulky pons, forming a recognisable pattern
Although first described in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of Quebec, ARSACS is now identified worldwide with a wide range of SACS variants
Other recessive spastic ataxias, including SPG7-related and metabolic causes, should be considered where the picture is atypical
Diagnosis combines the clinical triad, the characteristic MRI and retinal findings, and molecular confirmation, usually by sequencing or a gene panel
There is no cure; management is supportive, addressing spasticity, ataxia, neuropathy and mobility
reference.pathophysiology: ARSACS results from loss-of-function variants in SACS, which encodes sacsin, a very large multidomain protein with chaperone-like activity that supports protein folding and mitochondrial dynamics and distribution, and is important in Purkinje cells and in long motor and sensory axons. Deficiency of sacsin disturbs protein quality control and mitochondrial function, causing Purkinje cell abnormalities, corticospinal tract dysfunction and a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy. These combined effects produce the characteristic spastic, ataxic and neuropathic phenotype, and the broader group of recessive spastic ataxias reflects related disturbances of neuronal maintenance from other genes.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with cerebellar features, such as SPG7
Other recessive ataxias including ataxia with oculomotor apraxia and ataxia-telangiectasia
Cerebral palsy in young children presenting with spasticity and incoordination
Leukodystrophies affecting cerebellar and corticospinal pathways
Treatable metabolic ataxias such as vitamin E deficiency and cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify vermian atrophy, linear pontine hypointensities and a bulky pons
Nerve conduction studies to document the peripheral neuropathy
Optical coherence tomography or fundoscopy for retinal nerve fibre thickening
SACS sequencing by gene panel or exome, with copy-number analysis
Screening for treatable recessive ataxias (vitamin E level, plasma cholestanol)
Family history and consanguinity assessment to support recessive inheritance
redFlags: Rapid deterioration or regression suggesting an alternative or acquired disorder
Severe bulbar or respiratory involvement requiring supportive intervention
Cognitive decline or white-matter change raising the possibility of a leukodystrophy
A treatable metabolic mimic on screening (vitamin E deficiency or cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis) that must not be missed
reference.prognosis: ARSACS is progressive over years, and many affected individuals lose independent ambulation and become wheelchair-dependent in mid-adult life, with the tempo and severity varying by variant; other recessive spastic ataxias differ in course, so prognosis is best individualised once the specific gene is known.
pitfalls: Missing a treatable recessive mimic such as vitamin E deficiency or cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis before settling on ARSACS
Mislabelling a young child with spasticity and incoordination as having cerebral palsy
Overlooking the retinal and MRI clues that strongly suggest ARSACS
Not testing SACS or not recognising the broader recessive spastic ataxia group
Failing to address consanguinity and recessive inheritance in genetic counselling
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy is available, so management is supportive and centred on physiotherapy and occupational therapy to sustain gait and daily function
Treat pyramidal spasticity with oral antispasticity drugs such as baclofen or tizanidine, focal botulinum toxin injections and stretching
Fit ankle-foot orthoses and provide walking aids and podiatry for the length-dependent neuropathy and foot deformity
Offer balance and gait rehabilitation, falls prevention and speech-and-language therapy for dysarthria and swallowing
Monitor for orthopaedic complications such as pes cavus and scoliosis, and assess vision given the retinal involvement
Screen for and exclude treatable ataxia mimics such as vitamin E deficiency before settling on supportive care
Provide genetic counselling and family screening for autosomal recessive inheritance, coordinated by a neurology-led team
